title: Hourly Chauffeur or Separate Transfers? Planning a Day of Meetings
description: Compare hourly chauffeur service with separate transfers for a business day. Use sample itineraries and a booking checklist to choose the right fit.
cta: Plan the transportation around your day.
body:
A day with several meetings does not automatically need an hourly chauffeur. The useful question is whether you need a vehicle available between stops, or only a confirmed ride at specific times. That distinction can keep you from paying for availability you will not use, or discovering that a booked transfer does not cover the rest of your afternoon.

For a business visit to San Francisco or Silicon Valley, sketch the schedule first. Then compare the same itinerary as separate transfers and as an hourly booking. Here is how to make that comparison.

Start with what you need between meetings

A point-to-point transfer is arranged around an agreed pickup and destination. If you need a return ride, book that leg too; do not assume the vehicle waits after the first drop-off.

An hourly chauffeur booking reserves service for an agreed block of time. It can suit a changing sequence of stops, but the quote still needs a planned route, start and finish, and any applicable mileage or service-area limits. An hourly booking is not a promise of unlimited driving or unlimited changes.

Three schedules, three different decisions

One office, most of the day

Imagine arriving at SFO, spending six hours at a single office, then returning to a hotel. Separate arrival and evening transfers are worth pricing first. If you do not need the vehicle during the workday and can set the second pickup time, an hourly booking may reserve hours you will not use.

Several meetings with uncertain finish times

Now imagine meetings in San Francisco, San Mateo and Palo Alto, with lunch between appointments. Hourly service is worth comparing when you need continuity and expect the schedule to move. Give the operator every planned stop; the distance between meetings matters as much as the number of appointments.

These are planning examples, not promises that a particular sequence fits into a set number of hours. Allow for traffic, building access and the time it takes each passenger to reach the pickup location.

A short meeting day followed by an evening event

A mixed arrangement may fit better: an hourly block for the meetings and a separately booked evening transfer. Ask for both versions. A long break can change the comparison, and ending an hourly booking usually does not mean the same vehicle remains available later.

Compare complete quotes for the same itinerary

Comparing an hourly rate with a single transfer price misses the rest of the trip. Send one itinerary and ask what each complete option includes:

  • All planned legs: include the first pickup, intermediate stops and final destination.
  • Vehicle class and luggage: use the same class for both options and disclose suitcases, presentation equipment and other bulky items.
  • Time and distance: confirm any minimum hours, included mileage, additional mileage and where the service time begins and ends.
  • Schedule changes: ask how extra stops, extended time, waiting and a late-running final meeting are handled.
  • Included costs: confirm tolls, parking, airport fees and gratuity against the written quote.
  • Change and cancellation terms: review the terms that apply to the actual reservation.

A fixed quote gives you a price for an agreed booking. Changes to that booking can affect the total. Review Koast's current terms and your confirmation before making assumptions about extra waiting or an extended day.

Give the chauffeur usable pickup details

A building address is only part of a business pickup. If the office has more than one entrance, specify the one your passenger will use. Include the passenger's mobile number and a coordinator contact when someone else is booking.

For an airport arrival, include the flight number and arrival date, then follow the pickup instructions provided for the reservation. For an office departure, distinguish a firm departure deadline from an estimated meeting end. Let the operator know when plans change rather than assuming the driver can infer the new schedule.

A copy-and-send itinerary checklist

  • Travel date and passenger count.
  • Passenger name and mobile number; coordinator contact if different.
  • First pickup address, entrance and requested time.
  • Flight details for an airport arrival.
  • Every planned stop, in order, with appointment times.
  • Any firm arrival deadlines and uncertain meeting finish times.
  • Final drop-off and expected end time.
  • Vehicle preference, luggage and equipment.
  • Whether you need the vehicle available between stops.
  • Billing contact and receipt requirements.

Choose based on the day you actually have

Separate transfers are worth considering when pickups are predictable and you do not need a vehicle during the gaps. An hourly chauffeur is worth considering when several stops and changing finish times make ongoing availability useful. A combination can work when the day has a long break.
